messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 34-year-old parole officer who has been with his girlfriend for three years, though the relationship has grown distant in recent months. Three years ago, his ex-partner, a woman he had lived with for two years, became violent during an argument. She pinned him against the wall, her forearm pressed across his throat; he could smell the antiseptic hand sanitizer she had just used at her nursing job. She screamed that he was worthless, that no one would ever believe him. He remembers the taste of blood from his bitten lip, and even now, when the memory returns, he can taste that metallic saltiness as though it were fresh. The sound of her voice—the exact pitch and rhythm of her threats—sometimes plays in his head without warning, and the memory does not feel like something from the past; it feels as though he is back in that moment, pinned and helpless, his airway closing.

Kofi works in a downtown parole office, where he meets with formerly incarcerated men in a small, windowless room. The smell of the building’s industrial disinfectant hits him every time he walks through the door, and his body immediately goes on alert. His shoulders tighten, his jaw clenches, and he begins scanning the hallway for any man who might be standing too close or looking at him too long. He watches their hands, their posture, their eyes. When a parolee holds his gaze a second longer than expected, Kofi feels the memory surge—the taste of blood, the sound of her voice—and he becomes convinced that the man is about to attack. What happened to Kofi was deeply unfair, he believes, and nothing has been done about it; his ex-partner faced no consequences, and he has come to feel that his life has been destroyed by what she did. There are days when he is not sure his life is worth living anymore.

These appraisals drive much of Kofi’s behavior. Because he believes his life is already ruined, he has stopped pushing back against small provocations at work. He avoids any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, even when a parolee is clearly violating a condition of release. He has also begun avoiding eye contact with everyone—colleagues, strangers, his girlfriend—because looking someone in the eye feels like an invitation to be seen, and being seen feels dangerous. He pushes away positive emotions, too: when his girlfriend tries to hold his hand or tell him she loves him, he pulls back, because feeling good feels unsafe, as though any moment of softness will be punished.

The constant threat monitoring feeds back into itself. Kofi’s body is perpetually tense, ready to react, and this hypervigilance means he notices every potential danger—a man walking behind him in the parking lot, a stranger’s lingering glance. Each perceived threat triggers the memory again, and each memory reinforces his belief that the world is unsafe and that his life has been stolen. His avoidance strategies, in turn, make the memories more intrusive: by dodging eye contact and conflict, he never tests whether his fears are realistic, so the memory retains its power to feel present and real. And by avoiding positive feelings, he starves himself of any experience that might counter his negative appraisals.

The cycle tightened over months. Kofi began arriving late to work, claiming traffic, because the antiseptic smell in the lobby was unbearable. He stopped attending team meetings, citing caseload pressure, because sitting in a room full of men made his skin crawl. His supervisor noticed his avoidance of conflict and assigned him fewer high-risk cases, which Kofi interpreted as proof that he was failing. At home, his girlfriend stopped reaching for him; she told him he felt like a stranger. What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment in the parole office when a client—a large man with a quiet voice—said, “You okay, man?” and Kofi froze, tasted blood in his mouth, and could not speak for nearly a minute. He realized he could no longer do his job. He is afraid that therapy will not work, that he is too broken, but he is also afraid of what will happen if he does not try.
